q: Basically there are two main types of microscope, the light microscope and the electron microscope.
e: True. Basically there are two main types of microscope, the light microscope and the electron microscope. A light microscope uses light as the radiation that forms the image. Electron microscopes use electrons as the radiation source.

q: The light microscope uses electron as a source of radiation to form the image of the specimen.
e: False. A light microscope uses light, not electrons. Electrons are for electron microscopes.

q: The electron microscope uses electron as a source of radiation.
e: True. The electron microscope uses electron as a source of radiation. Electron microscopes use electrons as the radiation source. An electron microscope uses electrons, not light, and can magnify up to about 500,000 times.

q: Two different types of electron microscopes are commonly used: the transmission electron microscope (TEM) and the scanning electron microscope (SEM).
e: True. Two different types of electron microscopes are commonly used: the transmission electron microscope (TEM) and the scanning electron microscope (SEM). Electron microscopes use electrons as the radiation source. An electron microscope uses electrons, not light, and can magnify up to about 500,000 times.

q: In the TEM, the electron beam is passed back and forth over the surface of the specimen.
e: False. TEM does not scan back and forth over the surface. SEM does that; TEM sends electrons through a thin slice.

q: In the SEM, only the reflected beam is observed and a three dimensional appearance is obtained.
e: True. In the SEM, only the reflected beam is observed and a three dimensional appearance is obtained. Observed size over actual size gives magnification. Dichotomous does not mean divided into three parts.

q: In the light microscope, usually substage illumination is the light source.
e: True. In the light microscope, usually substage illumination is the light source. A light microscope uses light as the radiation that forms the image. A light microscope uses light and typically magnifies up to about 1500 to 2000 times, not 500,000.

q: By adjusting the condenser, the amount of light reaching the specimen is controlled.
e: False. The condenser focuses light on the specimen. The iris diaphragm controls how much light arrives.

q: The condenser focuses the light onto the specimen on the slide.
e: True. The condenser focuses the light onto the specimen on the slide. The condenser focuses light onto the specimen; an iris diaphragm controls how much light.

q: The objective lens is responsible for both the magnification and resolution.
e: True. The objective lens is responsible for both the magnification and resolution. Magnification is how many times larger the image is than the real object. Resolution is the ability to distinguish two close points as separate.

q: The eyepiece lens magnifies and resolves the image formed by the objective lens.
e: False. The eyepiece magnifies but does not provide resolving power. Resolution comes from the objective.

q: In the electron microscope, the electron beam, the specimen and the fluorescent screen must be in the vacuum.
e: True. In the electron microscope, the electron beam, the specimen and the fluorescent screen must be in the vacuum. Electron microscopes use electrons as the radiation source. An electron microscope uses electrons, not light, and can magnify up to about 500,000 times.

q: The electron gun and anode emit high velocity electron beam.
e: True. The electron gun and anode emit high velocity electron beam. Electron microscopes use an electron beam, not a light beam.

q: The condenser electromagnetic lens focuses the electron beam onto the specimen.
e: True. The condenser electromagnetic lens focuses the electron beam onto the specimen. The condenser focuses light onto the specimen; an iris diaphragm controls how much light. Electron microscopes use an electron beam, not a light beam.

q: The projector electromagnetic lenses focus and magnify the first image.
e: False. Objective electromagnetic lenses form and magnify the first image. Projector lenses throw that image onto the screen.

q: The image of the specimen in an electron microscope is recorded in black and white on the screen or photographic plate.
e: True. The image of the specimen in an electron microscope is recorded in black and white on the screen or photographic plate. Electron microscopes use electrons as the radiation source. An electron microscope uses electrons, not light, and can magnify up to about 500,000 times.

q: The light microscope magnifies up to 500,000X.
e: False. A light microscope does not reach 500,000 times. That order of magnification is for electron microscopes.

q: The electron microscope magnifies up to 500,000X.
e: True. The electron microscope magnifies up to 500,000X. Electron microscopes use electrons as the radiation source. An electron microscope uses electrons, not light, and can magnify up to about 500,000 times.

q: In a light microscope, either dead or alive specimen can be examined.
e: True. In a light microscope, either dead or alive specimen can be examined. A light microscope uses light as the radiation that forms the image. A light microscope uses light and typically magnifies up to about 1500 to 2000 times, not 500,000.

q: In an electron microscope, only dehydrated and dead specimen can be examined.
e: True. In an electron microscope, only dehydrated and dead specimen can be examined. Electron microscopes use electrons as the radiation source. An electron microscope uses electrons, not light, and can magnify up to about 500,000 times.

q: The preparation of specimen for an electron microscope is simple and not complicated.
e: False. Electron-microscope preparation is lengthy and complicated, not simple.

q: Magnification is the ability to increase the size of the image of the object being studied so that microscopic organisms become visible.
e: True. Magnification is the ability to increase the size of the image of the object being studied so that microscopic organisms become visible. Magnification is how many times larger the image is than the real object.

q: The formula for magnification is $M = \frac{A}{I}$ where $A$ is actual size and $I$ is observed size.
e: False. Magnification is observed image size divided by actual size, not actual divided by image.

q: Resolution is the ability to distinguish between two objects that are close together.
e: True. Resolution is the ability to distinguish between two objects that are close together. Dichotomous means divided into two parts, from Greek.

q: An increase in magnification always produces a more detailed image.
e: False. More magnification does not always mean more detail. Without resolution the image is only a larger blur.

q: With resolution, the greater the resolution, the greater the detail.
e: True. With resolution, the greater the resolution, the greater the detail. Resolution is the ability to distinguish two close points as separate.
